text: Ahl as-Sunnah (Ash'ari and Maturidi) teach that Allah exists without a body, form, limits, place or direction; He is not contained by the six directions as created things are, and nothing resembles Him (Qur'an 42:11). Verses such as Allah's 'istawa' over the Throne are affirmed as Allah stated them, while denying any bodily meaning: the early scholars consigned their meaning to Allah (tafwid) and later scholars also gave sound figurative interpretations (ta'wil), such as dominion. Imam al-Tahawi states that Allah is beyond limits, ends, parts and limbs.
src: al-Aqidah al-Tahawiyyah (Imam al-Tahawi), article on Allah's transcendence
al-Fiqh al-Akbar (attributed to Imam Abu Hanifa)

text: Allah is One in His essence, attributes and acts. His eternal attributes include life, knowledge, power, will, hearing, sight and speech (kalam); the Qur'an is the uncreated speech of Allah, while our recitation, ink and paper are created. The Maturidis also affirm the eternal attribute of bringing into being (takwin). His attributes are neither He nor other than He, and they do not resemble the attributes of creation.
src: Aqa'id al-Nasafi, section on the attributes

text: Iman is affirmation in the heart (tasdiq) of everything the Prophet ﷺ brought, with declaration by the tongue (iqrar). Major sins do not take a believer out of iman, and Ahl as-Sunnah do not declare anyone of the people of the qibla a disbeliever because of a sin unless they deem it lawful. A sinful believer is under Allah's will: He may forgive or punish, but no believer remains in the Fire forever.
src: al-Aqidah al-Tahawiyyah, articles on iman and the people of the qibla

text: Everything happens by Allah's knowledge, will, decree and creation, good and bad. Humans have a real choice and acquisition (kasb) for which they are accountable, while Allah alone creates their acts. Belief in qadr is one of the six pillars of iman (Hadith of Jibril). One should not use qadr as an excuse for sin; rather strive, make dua and be content with Allah's decree.
src: Aqa'id al-Nasafi, section on the acts of servants

topic: Prophets: infallibility and the finality of the Prophet ﷺ
text: All prophets are protected (ma'sum) from sins and from anything that would undermine their message. Muhammad ﷺ is the Seal of the Prophets (Qur'an 33:40): there is no prophet after him, so anyone claiming prophethood after him is a liar, and Ahl as-Sunnah regard the Qadiani/Ahmadi claim as outside Islam. The Isra and Mi'raj happened while awake, with body and soul. He ﷺ is the best of creation and his love is part of iman.
src: al-Aqidah al-Tahawiyyah, articles on prophethood and the Mi'raj
Sahih al-Bukhari 15 (love of the Prophet ﷺ)

text: Ahl as-Sunnah affirm the questioning in the grave by Munkar and Nakir, the reward and punishment of the grave, resurrection, the scale (mizan), the bridge (sirat), the Pool (hawd), and the intercession of the Prophet ﷺ, the prophets, scholars, martyrs and the righteous by Allah's permission, including for people of major sins. The believers will see Allah in Paradise without modality or direction.
src: Sunan al-Tirmidhi 2435 (intercession for people of major sins)

text: Ahl as-Sunnah love all the Companions and the Ahl al-Bayt and speak of them only with good. The best of the Ummah after the Prophet ﷺ are Abu Bakr, then Umar, then Uthman, then Ali (Allah be pleased with them), the rightly guided caliphs. The disputes among the Companions are not used to insult any of them; love of the Ahl al-Bayt is part of the deen.
src: al-Aqidah al-Tahawiyyah, articles on the Companions

text: The awliya are the God-fearing believers whom Allah loves (Qur'an 10:62-63). Their karamat (miracles granted by Allah) are true and affirmed by Ahl as-Sunnah, such as the provision that came to Maryam (Qur'an 3:37) and the throne of Bilqis brought by one who had knowledge of the Book (Qur'an 27:40). A wali never reaches the rank of a prophet, and no wali is free from following the Shari'ah.

topic: Following a madhhab (taqlid) and the four schools
text: Ahl as-Sunnah wal-Jama'ah follow one of the four schools of fiqh: Hanafi (Imam Abu Hanifa), Maliki (Imam Malik), Shafi'i (Imam al-Shafi'i) and Hanbali (Imam Ahmad). All four are valid paths drawn from the Qur'an, Sunnah, consensus and analogy; their differences are a mercy and should be respected. A lay Muslim follows a qualified school (taqlid) rather than deriving rulings directly, and does not pick easy opinions from different schools out of desire (talfiq for convenience). In belief, the Ash'ari and Maturidi schools represent Ahl as-Sunnah.
src: Imam al-Nawawi, al-Majmu', introduction on taqlid

text: Tasawwuf is the science of ihsan: 'to worship Allah as though you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He sees you' (Hadith of Jibril). It purifies the heart (tazkiyah) from pride, envy, showing off and love of the world, and adorns it with sincerity, repentance, patience, gratitude, trust and love of Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, always within the Shari'ah. Imam al-Ghazali's Ihya Ulum al-Din and Imam al-Qushayri's Risala are foundational texts.

topic: Spiritual stations: tawbah, sabr, shukr, tawakkul, rida
text: Imam al-Qushayri describes the path as stations: sincere repentance (tawbah) with regret, quitting the sin and resolve not to return; scrupulousness (wara'); detachment from the world (zuhd); patience (sabr) in obedience, away from sin and in trials; gratitude (shukr) with heart, tongue and limbs; trust in Allah (tawakkul) while taking means; and contentment (rida) with Allah's decree. Imam al-Ghazali devotes the 'Saving Matters' quarter of the Ihya to these virtues.
src: al-Risala al-Qushayriyya, chapters on tawbah, sabr, tawakkul and rida

text: Dhikr is the life of the heart: 'Remember Me and I will remember you' (Qur'an 2:152) and 'In the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest' (13:28). Sending salawat on the Prophet ﷺ is commanded (33:56). Gatherings of dhikr are praised in hadith (Sahih Muslim 2689). The Sufi orders (Qadiriyya, Chishtiyya, Naqshbandiyya, Suhrawardiyya) transmit dhikr and adab through an authorised murshid by bay'ah, who must himself follow the Shari'ah and Sunnah.
src: Sahih Muslim 2689 (angels seeking gatherings of dhikr)

text: Celebrating the Mawlid (birth) of the Prophet ﷺ with Qur'an, salawat, his sirah, na'ts, charity and feeding people is a praiseworthy practice (bid'ah hasanah) according to many great Sunni scholars. Evidences include rejoicing in Allah's mercy (Qur'an 10:58; the Prophet ﷺ is a mercy, 21:107) and the Prophet ﷺ fasting on Mondays because 'that is the day I was born' (Sahih Muslim 1162). Imam al-Suyuti wrote Husn al-Maqsid fi Amal al-Mawlid in its support, and Hafiz Ibn Hajar derived a basis for it from the Ashura fast. It must be free of anything against the Shari'ah.
src: Imam al-Suyuti, Husn al-Maqsid fi Amal al-Mawlid
Imam Ahmad Rida Khan, Fatawa Ridawiyya (Mawlid)

topic: Tawassul through the Prophet ﷺ and the righteous
text: Tawassul (asking Allah by means of the Prophet ﷺ, the righteous or one's good deeds) is permitted according to Ahl as-Sunnah: Allah says 'seek the means (wasilah) to Him' (Qur'an 5:35). The Prophet ﷺ taught the blind man to pray: 'O Allah, I ask You and turn to You through Your Prophet Muhammad, the Prophet of mercy...' (Sunan al-Tirmidhi 3578; Sunan Ibn Majah 1385). Umar sought rain through al-Abbas (Sahih al-Bukhari 1010). The believer knows that Allah alone creates and grants; the means are honoured by Allah.

topic: Visiting graves (ziyarah) and the Prophet's ﷺ resting place
text: Visiting graves is a Sunnah: 'I had forbidden you from visiting graves; now visit them' (Sahih Muslim 977), as it reminds of the hereafter. One greets the deceased, recites Qur'an and makes dua for them. Visiting the blessed resting place of the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah is among the greatest acts of nearness, as the scholars of all four schools state in their chapters on Hajj, and visiting the shrines of the awliya with adab is accepted, while avoiding any un-Islamic acts.
src: Imam al-Nawawi, al-Adhkar and al-Idah fi Manasik al-Hajj (ziyarah of the Prophet ﷺ)

text: Gifting the reward of good deeds (Qur'an, charity, feeding people) to the deceased (Isal-e-Thawab) reaches them by Allah's grace: a man gave charity for his deceased mother with the Prophet's ﷺ approval (Sahih al-Bukhari 1388; Sahih Muslim 1004). Gyarhween Sharif is Isal-e-Thawab gatherings on the 11th of the month (especially Rabi al-Akhir) for Shaykh Abdul Qadir Jilani. Urs is the annual remembrance of a wali with Qur'an, dhikr, salawat, a talk and charity. These are accepted practices in the Sunni-Sufi tradition when kept free of un-Islamic acts.
src: Imam Ahmad Rida Khan, Fatawa Ridawiyya (Isal-e-Thawab, fatiha)
Sadr al-Shari'ah Amjad Ali Azmi, Bahar-e-Shariat (fatiha and Isal-e-Thawab)
